Object
ub-JEKT (v.); OB-jekt (n.)
v.i. (to state an argument against; to raise a charge or accusation); n. (a thing presented to the mind or senses)
Latin objectus, past participle of objicere, to throw against, from ob-, against, and jacere, to throw. To object is, at root, to throw a charge against someone, setting an accusation in their path.

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version's one use of the word as a verb belongs to Paul's defense before Felix, and it appears in a sentence whose whole force depends on something conspicuously missing. Paul lists the Jews of Asia who had originally stirred up the temple crowd against him, and points out that they, of all people, are absent from this very trial where the actual accusation is being made: Who ought to have been here before thee, and object, if they had ought against me. The men best positioned to bring a real objection, having witnessed whatever supposedly happened, have not come; the charge is instead being pressed secondhand by others with no direct testimony to offer.

The verse works as a piece of careful legal argument, not merely a complaint. Paul does not simply deny the accusation; he names precisely who should have appeared to object, under Roman legal expectation, and lets their absence speak for itself. It is the same instinct Scripture elsewhere commends in Deuteronomy's law of witnesses, that no man should be condemned on hearsay where the actual accusers will not stand and object to his face. Paul's confidence before Felix rests not on rhetorical flourish but on the plain fact that no one qualified to object has been willing to do so under oath.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): to oppose in words or arguments; to offer as a charge or ground of opposition; to bring forward as an accusation.

expand to see more

OBJECT, v.i. To offer reasons or arguments against; to make a charge or accusation, especially before a tribunal.

ACCUSE, v.t. To charge with a crime or fault; to bring a formal accusation against.

WITNESS, n. One who testifies to a fact from personal knowledge; one who gives evidence in a legal proceeding.

TESTIMONY, n. Evidence given by a witness, under oath, concerning a matter of fact.

TRIBUNAL, n. A court of justice; the seat of a judge; a place where judgment is administered.

Key Scripture

Act 24:13 — "Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me."

Act 24:19 — "Who ought to have been here before thee, and object, if they had ought against me."

Act 25:11 — "For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar."

Deu 19:15 — "One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established."

Modern Corruption

An accusation is treated as credible simply for having been made loudly or repeatedly, when Paul's own defense turns on the specific, legally trained observation that the men who could actually object under oath have declined to appear at all.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word; to object still means to raise a stated charge against someone. The principle worth recovering is Paul's own discipline in constructing his defense: he does not merely assert his innocence, he identifies the specific procedural gap in the case against him, that the original accusers who stirred up the crowd in Asia are conspicuously not present to object in person.

Deuteronomy's law of witnesses supplies the standing biblical principle behind that discipline — no man condemned on the word of one witness, let alone on secondhand report from men unwilling to appear and object directly. Paul's confidence before both Felix and later before Festus, culminating in his appeal to Caesar, is not the confidence of a man daring the system to catch him, but of a man who has checked that the system's own rules of evidence have not actually been met against him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek enkaleo (G1458), to call in, to accuse, to bring charges; the verb behind “object” in Acts 24:19, a legal term for lodging a formal complaint.

expand to see more

Greek enkaleo (G1458) — to call to account, to accuse, to bring a legal charge; the verb rendered “object” in Acts 24:19.

Greek kategoreo (G2723) — to accuse, to speak against; the more common verb used of Paul's accusers throughout Acts 24-25.

Greek apologeomai (G626) — to speak in one's own defense; the standing verb of Paul's own legal responses in this section.

Greek epikaleomai (G1941) — to call upon, to appeal; the verb behind Paul's appeal to Caesar in Acts 25:11.

Hebrew ed (H5707) — a witness; the office Deuteronomy 19:15 requires in plural before any charge can stand.

Usage

"“Who ought to have been here before thee, and object, if they had ought against me” — Paul's pointed observation of his accusers' absence."

"“Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me” — the substance of Paul's defense."

"“At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” — the law of evidence behind it."
